title: What Were the BONE WARS?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Bone Wars, the bitter 1870s-1890s rivalry between American paleontologists Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh. They trace early American paleontology from Lewis and Clark and Joseph Leidy, through the Hadrosaurus foulkii find in New Jersey, to the friendship's breakdown (the Elasmosaurus head-on-tail mistake, Marsh's bribing of Cope's diggers), the race to fossil fields opened by the Transcontinental Railroad, the 1877 winter digs that produced Triceratops and Stegosaurus, the Brontosaurus/Apatosaurus naming story, Cope's financial ruin, Marsh's attempt to seize Cope's collection, the New York Herald article and Congressional budget cuts, and both men's deaths. The episode closes with listener mail about the Civil Air Patrol.
topics: U.S. Geological Survey fossil collection seizure

entities.name: Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia

segments.title: Tour dates and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh announces upcoming tour dates and the hosts banter about dinosaur interests as kids and a dinosaur-obsessed generation. They tease the 1877 origins of American dinosaur interest and compare it to Tesla and Edison.

segments.title: Bone Wars movie and title
segments.summary: The hosts mention a canceled movie about the Bone Wars that was to star Steve Carell and James Gandolfini, which fell apart after Gandolfini's death, and note the title was already used by adult films.

segments.title: Early American paleontology and Lewis and Clark
segments.summary: The hosts describe early fossil collecting, Lewis and Clark's fossil excavation near a salt lick, and the early American paleontologists Edward Hitchcock and Joseph Leidy.

segments.title: Hadrosaurus discovery and Leidy
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1858 Hadrosaurus foulkii find in New Jersey, the first major East Coast dinosaur skeleton, which Leidy was called in to excavate. They describe Leidy as a steady, reliable founding figure of American paleontology.

segments.title: Marsh's background
segments.summary: The hosts profile Othniel Charles Marsh, born in New York to a farming family, whose wealthy uncle George Peabody funded his education at Yale and Germany and secured him a professorship at the new Peabody Museum.

segments.title: Cope's background and gentleman naturalists
segments.summary: Edward Drinker Cope came from a wealthy Philadelphia family, dropped out of high school at sixteen, and followed the gentleman naturalist tradition. The hosts contrast his flowery writing with Marsh's dry style and discuss their religious and evolutionary views, including neo-Lamarckism.

segments.title: Friendship, Haddonfield dig and the Elasmosaurus mistake
segments.summary: Cope and Marsh first became friends in Germany in 1863. Marsh visited Cope's Haddonfield dig, secretly bribed the diggers to send fossils to him, and then pointed out that Cope's Elasmosaurus skeleton had its head on the tail end, which humiliated Cope.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the discussion of what Marsh said ended the friendship.

segments.title: The Western fields and the rivalry escalates
segments.summary: The hosts describe how the Transcontinental Railroad opened the American West's rich fossil fields. Marsh was first to the West and treated it as his turf. Cope sold his family farm and funded his own expeditions, while Marsh relied on Yale and government funding.
topics: Native American resistance to westward expansion

segments.title: Prolific publishing and the American Naturalist
segments.summary: Cope published roughly 1,400 papers, many in a short span, and bought the American Naturalist journal in 1877 to publish his own work, which drained his finances. Marsh published fewer but more prestigious papers. Sloppy taxonomy resulted from the rush to name species.

segments.title: Dirty tactics, the 1877 winter dig and Brontosaurus naming
segments.summary: The hosts describe the rivals' sabotage, poaching, and smashing of fossils, and the 1877 winter digs that yielded Triceratops, Stegosaurus, and Apatosaurus. They discuss the Apatosaurus versus Brontosaurus naming issue and whether the sabotage stories are exaggerated.

segments.title: Marsh seizes Cope's collection and the final downfall
segments.summary: Marsh, now at the U.S. Geological Survey, cut off Cope's government funding and tried to seize his collection under a law he had introduced, which Cope successfully contested. Cope went to the New York Herald, leading Congress to cut the USGS budget and costing Marsh his position and part of his own collection. Cope died in 1897 and Marsh in 1899.

segments.title: Listener mail: Civil Air Patrol
segments.summary: A listener named Jackson, a senior master sergeant in the Civil Air Patrol, praises the show's Civil Air Patrol episode and asks for a shout out to his Green Mountain Composite Squadron. The hosts also ask for more on cadet life.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and direct listeners to the website and email address.
